did_you_know.text: Psalm 95 opens with a public invitation to sing and shout to the LORD, who is described as “the Rock of our salvation”—a steadfast source of deliverance.
Praise to the LORD is described in several ways: coming before him with thanksgiving and shouting to him with songs, combining gratitude and singing in worship.
The LORD is called “the great God” and “the great King above all gods,” expressions that emphasize his greatness and supremacy.
The psalm describes the LORD’s rule over all the earth: the depths of the earth are in his hand, and the mountain peaks belong to him.
Both the sea and the dry land belong to the LORD: the sea is his because he made it, and the dry land was formed by his hands.
The call to worship the LORD includes three gestures of submission: bowing down, kneeling, and prostrating ourselves before him, our Maker.
Israel is described as “the people of his pasture” and “the flock under his care”—a people and flock guided by him. Immediately afterward comes the call to hear his voice “today.”
The psalm warns against hardening the heart and recalls Meribah and Massah in the wilderness as examples of how the people tested the LORD.

The criticism of Israel’s ancestors is that they tested and tried the LORD even though they had seen his works. Thus, the psalm connects witnessing God’s deeds with the responsibility to listen to him.
The psalm concludes by recalling forty years of wandering, a generation described as straying in heart and not knowing the LORD’s ways. As a result, the LORD swore that they would not enter his rest.
